B.5 Discrete symmetry action on monopoles

The elementary flux-reversing IR operations exchange monopoles and antimonopoles. In the conventions used below we choose

𝒯IR\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\rm IR} :ΦA→EA​B​ΦB†,\displaystyle:\ \Phi_{A}\rightarrow E_{AB}\Phi_{B}^{\dagger}, (147)
ℛIR\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\rm IR} :ΦA→EA​B​ΦB†,\displaystyle:\ \Phi_{A}\rightarrow E_{AB}\Phi_{B}^{\dagger}, (148)
𝒞IR\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rm IR} :ΦA→ΦA†.\displaystyle:\ \Phi_{A}\rightarrow\Phi_{A}^{\dagger}. (149)

Here Hermitian conjugation converts the lower SU​(12)f\mathrm{SU}(12)_{f} index into the conjugate representation, and the invariant tensor EE returns it to the lower-index convention. The microscopic time-reversal operation also reverses U​(1)top\mathrm{U}(1)_{\rm top} charge: it contains the physical Kramers spin rotation together with the opposite-valley and Dirac-spinor actions in Eq. (25). Its action on charge-one coefficient vectors is therefore classified only after Hermitian conjugation and EE-dualization, through the linear map 𝖠𝒯\mathsf{A}_{\mathcal{T}} of Eq. (122).

Appendix C The U(1)top action of GUV symmetries

C.1 Berry phase of time-reversal

Since the U​(1)top\mathrm{U}(1)_{\mathrm{top}} phase is an inherently UV phenomenon, we trivialize the IR QED3 by adding a quantum spin Hall mass term [63],

δ​ℒ=m​ψ¯i​σz​ψj,m>0,\delta\mathcal{L}=m\overline{\psi}_{i}\sigma_{z}\psi_{j}\,,\quad m>0\,, (150)

which gaps out the spinons, leaving pure Maxwell gauge theory in the IR. The zero-mode degeneracy of the monopoles is also lifted, leaving a unique light monopole Φlight\Phi_{\mathrm{light}} in which all six valley zero-modes are occupied with spin ↓\downarrow; this assignment is fixed by symmetry. The mass term breaks the flavor symmetry down to SU⁡(12)→SO⁡(2)×…\mathrm{SU}(12)\rightarrow\mathrm{SO}(2)\times\dots, where SO⁡(2)\mathrm{SO}(2) is the conserved spin along the zz-axis. Probing the theory (or weakly gauging the SO⁡(2)\mathrm{SO}(2)) with an SO⁡(2)\mathrm{SO}(2) gauge field 𝒜SO⁡(2)\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{SO}(2)}, the massive fermions will generate a topological term

ℒtop=32​π​𝒜SO⁡(2)∧d​a,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{top}}=\frac{3}{2\pi}\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{SO}(2)}\wedge\mathrm{d}a\,, (151)

which means the monopole carries charge 33 under SO⁡(2)\mathrm{SO}(2) (and is a singlet under the rest of the unbroken flavor symmetry). Now in this regime, we can calculate the Berry phase of light monopole in this theory, from which by SU⁡(12)\mathrm{SU}(12) rotations, we can find the transformations of the other monopoles.

The added mass δ​ℒ\delta\mathcal{L} leads to a quantum spin Hall insulating state. A single quantum spin Hall insulator is a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} topological insulator [41] protected by Kramers time reversal. In the convention used here, a single copy takes the corresponding light monopole to minus its Hermitian conjugate. Because the maple-leaf theory contains three such copies, the reference spin-33, valley-singlet monopole obeys

𝒯​Φlight​𝒯−1=−Φlight†.\mathcal{T}\Phi_{\rm light}\mathcal{T}^{-1}=-\Phi_{\rm light}^{\dagger}. (152)

The same sign is consistent with the topological response in Eq. (151), for which a charge-one monopole carries spin 33. This fixes the overall reference phase used in the coefficient map 𝖠𝒯\mathsf{A}_{\mathcal{T}} of Eq. (122). The physically important statement is that microscopic time reversal reverses U​(1)top\mathrm{U}(1)_{\rm top} charge; the 924×924924\times 924 matrix diagonalized in the classification is the dualized linear map on charge-one coefficient vectors, not a physical time-reversal endomorphism of the q=+1q=+1 operator space.

C.2 Details of the Wannier center decomposition

We determine the space-group Berry phases by decomposing the gapped spinon bands, after adding a small quantum spin Hall mass, into Wannier-center representations [63]. Concretely, this is done by computing the eigenvalues of rotations at high-symmetry points in momentum space. The U​(1)top\mathrm{U}(1)_{\mathrm{top}} phase can then be thought of as arising from the Aharonov-Bohm phase acquired by a monopole moving in the insulating charge background of the Fermi sea. A Wannier insulator of charge qrq_{r} centered at a rotation center rr means that for a CnC_{n} rotation around rr, a monopole will pick up a phase ei​qr​2​π/ne^{iq_{r}2\pi/n}. The Berry phase associated with translation symmetry can be determined by decomposing translation into compositions of rotations. As the spinon bands are gapless, we add a small quantum spin Hall mass perturbation to gap out the bands. Such a mass will not affect the monopole quantum numbers under the spatial symmetries and can be implemented by adding a directed imaginary hopping along the ttt_{t} bonds, with opposite signs for the two spin species.

We compare the resulting spinon band insulator to a basis of Wannier insulators on the maple-leaf lattice. To begin, we observe the maple-leaf lattice space group is p​6p6, generated by two translations T1,2T_{1,2} and C6C_{6} rotation around a hexagonal plaquette. The relevant high-symmetry momenta (in reciprocal lattice units) are 𝚪=(0,0)\bm{\Gamma}=(0,0), 𝑲=(13,13)\bm{K}=(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3}), 𝑲′=C6​(𝑲)\bm{K}^{\prime}=C_{6}(\bm{K}) and 𝑴=(12,0)\bm{M}=(\frac{1}{2},0).

We denote by ΓPSG\Gamma^{\rm PSG} the formal band representation of the occupied spinon bands of the PSG mean-field Hamiltonian, after adding the small quantum spin Hall mass used to gap the Dirac nodes. Equivalently, ΓPSG\Gamma^{\rm PSG} is the Wannier-center charge background of the filled spinon sea, expressed as an integer linear combination of elementary atomic band representations. This charge background is the object whose rotation-center charges determine the U​(1)top\mathrm{U}(1)_{\rm top} Berry phases of monopoles.

The possible p​6p6 Wannier centers are the usual ones centered on the C6C_{6} center (hexagon), C3C_{3} centers (triangular plaquettes defined by the ttt_{t} bonds), C2C_{2} centers (the tdt_{d} bond centers), and the physical sites, which form a C6C_{6} orbit. Accordingly, we analyze the Wannier insulators centered on the hexagonal plaquettes (Γh)(\Gamma^{h}), triangular plaquettes (Γt)(\Gamma^{t}), bond centers (Γe)(\Gamma^{e}), and sites (Γv)(\Gamma^{v}). The representation of Γv\Gamma^{v} is immediate, since it is the original tight-binding basis. For the other insulators, we represent them by taking equal-amplitude superpositions of spinons at the boundary sites of the relevant plaquette/triangle/bond.

We consider the eigenvalues under the original rotation C6,hC_{6,h} (in addition to C3​hC_{3h} and C2​hC_{2h}). There is also rotation around a C3C_{3} triangular plaquette, C3​tC_{3t}, and rotation around a C2C_{2} bond, C2​eC_{2e}. However, we do not consider these operations as they are related to C6,hC_{6,h} by translation and do not provide additional information. For more complicated PSGs or enlarged unit cells, simply matching eigenvalues may not be sufficient; one should in principle compare the full space-group or PSG representation.

We derive how to extract these eigenvalues in the general case. Given eigenvectors of the second quantized Hamiltonian hh,

h⁡(k)​ξn​(k)=En​(k)​ξn​(k),h(k)\xi_{n}(k)=E_{n}(k)\xi_{n}(k)\,, (153)

we can collect the occupied eigenvectors in Ξ⁡(k)=(ξ1​(k),…,ξNocc​(k))\Xi(k)=(\xi_{1}(k),\dots,\xi_{N_{\rm occ}}(k)). For a symmetry gg that acts on the spinon Bloch operators as

g​fk​g−1=Dg​(k)​fg​k,gf_{k}g^{-1}=D_{g}(k)f_{gk}\,, (154)

the matrix Dg​(k)D_{g}(k) is the single-particle symmetry matrix in the spinon Bloch basis. It includes the sublattice permutation, the associated Bloch phase factors, and the projective gauge transformation required by the PSG action of gg. The induced action of gg on the annihilation operators of the occupied bands is then

Ξ†​(k)​fk→Ξ†​(k)​Dg​(k)​fg​k=Ξ†​(k)​Dg​(k)​Ξ​(g​k)​[Ξ†​(g​k)​fg​k].\begin{split}\Xi^{\dagger}(k)f_{k}&\rightarrow\Xi^{\dagger}(k)D_{g}(k)f_{gk}\\ &\qquad=\Xi^{\dagger}(k)D_{g}(k)\Xi(gk)\left[\Xi^{\dagger}(gk)f_{gk}\right]\,.\end{split} (155)

Equivalently, the occupied-band wavefunctions transform with the matrix

Ξ†​(g​k)​Dg​(k)†​Ξ​(k).\Xi^{\dagger}(gk)D_{g}(k)^{\dagger}\Xi(k)\,. (156)

Diagonalizing this matrix at symmetry-invariant momenta, or within the appropriate little group of kk, yields the symmetry eigenvalues of the occupied spinon bands.

Let

Ω=e2​π​i/6,ω=e2​π​i/3=Ω2.\Omega=e^{2\pi i/6},\qquad\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}=\Omega^{2}. (157)

The hexagon-centered Wannier representations are denoted by Γηh\Gamma^{h}_{\eta}, where η∈ℤ6\eta\in\mathbb{Z}_{6} labels the intrinsic C6​hC_{6h} angular momentum, so that a Wannier orbital at the hexagon center transforms with eigenvalue Ωη\Omega^{\eta} under C6​hC_{6h}. Similarly, Γηt\Gamma^{t}_{\eta}, with η∈ℤ3\eta\in\mathbb{Z}_{3}, denotes a Wannier representation centered on the triangular plaquettes, with intrinsic C3​tC_{3t} angular momentum ωη\omega^{\eta}. Since, C6​hC_{6h} exchanges the two triangular plaquette centers in a unit cell, Γηt\Gamma^{t}_{\eta} is a two-band representation. At the Γ\Gamma point, for example, the corresponding C6​hC_{6h} action takes the form

(01ωη​ei​𝐤⋅𝐚10).\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ \omega^{\eta}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{a}_{1}}&0\end{pmatrix}. (158)

This gives the C6​hC_{6h} eigenvalues {Ωη,Ωη+3}\{\Omega^{\eta},\Omega^{\eta+3}\}. The bond-centered representations are denoted by Γle\Gamma^{e}_{l}, where l∈ℤ2l\in\mathbb{Z}_{2} labels the intrinsic C2​eC_{2e} angular momentum (−1)l(-1)^{l}. Finally, Γv\Gamma^{v} denotes the atomic representation obtained from Wannier orbitals on the six physical sites, which form a single C6C_{6} orbit. For these bond-centered representations, we write λ=(−1)l\lambda=(-1)^{l}. The rotation eigenvalues of these elementary Wannier-center representations are listed in Table 4.

Diagonalization of the spinon Hamiltonian leads to the representation of the spinon bands, shown in Table 5. As expected, we can see that from the product of the eigenvalues ξC6​h​ξC3​h​ξC2​h≠1\xi_{C_{6h}}\xi_{C_{3h}}\xi_{C_{2h}}\neq 1, the spinon bands for a single sector are topological and cannot be decomposed in terms of Wannier insulators. Instead, the occupied bands exhibit fragile topology [56]; even though they are topologically trivial in the strictest sense, they can be deformed into a Wannier limit only after being combined with another atomic insulator.

We now determine ΓPSG\Gamma^{\rm PSG} by matching the rotation eigenvalues of the occupied spinon bands in Table 5 to the elementary Wannier-center representations in Table 4. This matching is a linear problem in the integer coefficients of the atomic representations. One convenient solution is

ΓPSG=2​Γ0h+Γ1h−Γ3h+Γ5h−Γ0e+Γv.\Gamma^{\rm PSG}=2\Gamma^{h}_{0}+\Gamma^{h}_{1}-\Gamma^{h}_{3}+\Gamma^{h}_{5}-\Gamma^{e}_{0}+\Gamma^{v}. (167)

The equality here is meant at the level of the space-group rotation eigenvalue data. Indeed, the right-hand side gives the C6​hC_{6h} eigenvalues

⊕2{1,Ω,Ω−1}\oplus^{2}\{1,\Omega,\Omega^{-1}\}

at Γ\Gamma, the C3​hC_{3h} eigenvalues

⊕2{1,ω,ω2}\oplus^{2}\{1,\omega,\omega^{2}\}

at KK and K′K^{\prime}, and the C2​hC_{2h} eigenvalues

⊕2{−1,1,1}\oplus^{2}\{-1,1,1\}

at MM, in agreement with Table 5.

The decomposition in Eq. (167) assigns a net effective gauge charge qC6​h=3q_{C_{6h}}=3 to the hexagon-centered C6C_{6} rotation center, modulo six. Therefore, a 2​π2\pi monopole acquires the Berry phase

exp⁡(2​π​i​qC6​h6)=exp⁡(i​π)=−1\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi iq_{C_{6h}}}{6}\right)=\exp(i\pi)=-1 (168)

under C6​hC_{6h}. The translation Berry phases are trivial. For example, using T1=C3​t​C6​h4T_{1}=C_{3t}C_{6h}^{4}, the C6​h4C_{6h}^{4} contribution is exp⁡(2​π​i​qC6​h​ 4/6)=1\exp(2\pi i\,q_{C_{6h}}\,4/6)=1, and there is no net C3​tC_{3t}-centered charge contribution. Similarly, T2=C2​h​C2​eT_{2}=C_{2h}C_{2e} gives a trivial phase because the two C2C_{2} rotation-center contributions cancel modulo two.

The decomposition in Eq. (167) is not unique. The reason is that the rotation eigenvalues in Tables 4 and 5 do not distinguish certain combinations of atomic representations. In particular, the following differences have identical rotation eigenvalue data at the high-symmetry momenta:

∑η=02Γηt−∑η=05Γηh,Γ0e+Γ1e−∑η=05Γηh,Γv−∑η=05Γηh.\sum_{\eta=0}^{2}\Gamma^{t}_{\eta}-\sum_{\eta=0}^{5}\Gamma^{h}_{\eta},\qquad\Gamma^{e}_{0}+\Gamma^{e}_{1}-\sum_{\eta=0}^{5}\Gamma^{h}_{\eta},\qquad\Gamma^{v}-\sum_{\eta=0}^{5}\Gamma^{h}_{\eta}. (169)

Thus, one may add

a⁡(∑η=02Γηt−∑η=05Γηh)+b⁡(Γ0e+Γ1e−∑η=05Γηh)\displaystyle a\left(\sum_{\eta=0}^{2}\Gamma^{t}_{\eta}-\sum_{\eta=0}^{5}\Gamma^{h}_{\eta}\right)+b\left(\Gamma^{e}_{0}+\Gamma^{e}_{1}-\sum_{\eta=0}^{5}\Gamma^{h}_{\eta}\right) (170)
+c⁡(Γv−∑η=05Γηh).\displaystyle+c\left(\Gamma^{v}-\sum_{\eta=0}^{5}\Gamma^{h}_{\eta}\right).

where a,b,ca,b,c are arbitrary integers. Adding such a combination does not change the rotation eigenvalues used in the matching. This non-uniqueness does not affect the monopole Berry phases, because these phases depend only on the rotation-center charges modulo the corresponding rotation order: qC6​hq_{C_{6h}} modulo 66, qC3​tq_{C_{3t}} modulo 33, and qC2​eq_{C_{2e}} modulo 22. Each of the three differences in Eq. (170) changes these charges only by multiples of the corresponding rotation order. The three differences displayed in Eq. (170) are in fact a complete integral basis of the ambiguity. Writing the six hh-center coefficients, three tt-center coefficients, two ee-center coefficients, and the vv coefficient as a twelve-component integer vector, the matching matrix for the six Γ\Gamma-point C6C_{6} multiplicities, three KK-point C3C_{3} multiplicities, and two MM-point C2C_{2} multiplicities has rank nine. Exact integer row reduction leaves three free variables and gives the three generators in Eq. (170) as a saturated basis of the kernel. Their changes in the effective charges at the (C6,C3,C2)(C_{6},C_{3},C_{2}) centers are respectively

(−6,3,0),(−6,0,2),(−6,0,0),(-6,3,0),\qquad(-6,0,2),\qquad(-6,0,0), (171)

which vanish in ℤ6⊕ℤ3⊕ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{6}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{3}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{2}. The translation phases are independent of the ambiguity as well. For T1=C3​t​C6​h4T_{1}=C_{3t}C_{6h}^{4}, the change of the phase exponent is

δ​ν1=δ​Qt3+4​δ​Qh6,\delta\nu_{1}=\frac{\delta Q_{t}}{3}+\frac{4\,\delta Q_{h}}{6}, (172)

and for T2=C2​h​C2​eT_{2}=C_{2h}C_{2e} it is

δ​ν2=δ​Qh2+δ​Qe2.\delta\nu_{2}=\frac{\delta Q_{h}}{2}+\frac{\delta Q_{e}}{2}. (173)

For each of the three kernel generators these quantities are integers. Hence every rotation and translation Berry phase, including all relative signs, is independent of the arbitrary integers a,b,ca,b,c.

l=remarks,type=example,Name-sg=Example,name-sg=example,Name-pl=Examples,name-pl=examples,type=algorithm,Name-sg=Algorithm,name-sg=algorithm,Name-pl=Algorithms,name-pl=algorithms,type=listing,Name-sg=Listing,name-sg=listing,Name-pl=Listings,name-pl=listings,type=exercise,Name-sg=Exercise,name-sg=exercise,Name-pl=Exercises,name-pl=exercises,type=solution,Name-sg=Solution,name-sg=solution,Name-pl=Solutions,name-pl=solutions\seq_gput_right:Neenglish\msg_info:nnezref-cleverlangfile-loadedenglish\tl_put_left:Ne?? shows a DSL that is a distinct phase from the DSL considered in the main text. In particular, this DSL has two low-energy Dirac nodes at 𝚪\bm{\Gamma}, so its IR is described by Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3. For completeness, we perform a similar analysis of its monopoles and instabilities. The instability at the mean-field level refers to the absence of symmetry protection for the Dirac nodes at Γ\Gamma: generic allowed changes of the hopping parameters move the system away from this fine-tuned band touching and open a gap.

The lattice symmetries act on the Dirac fermions as

T1,2\displaystyle T_{1,2} :ψ→ψ,\displaystyle\;:\;\psi\rightarrow\psi\,, (178)
C6\displaystyle C_{6} :ψ→iμze−iπρz/6ψ,\displaystyle\;:\;\psi\rightarrow i\mu_{z}e^{-i\pi\rho_{z}/6}\psi\,, (179)
𝒯\displaystyle\mathcal{T} :ψ→i​σy​μy​ρy​ψ.\displaystyle\;:\;\psi\rightarrow i\sigma_{y}\mu_{y}\rho_{y}\psi\,. (180)

Here, ρ\rho acts on the two-component Dirac spinor structure, while μ\mu acts on the two-valley/node space of the Nf=4N_{f}=4 DSL.

The filled bands in the presence of a quantum spin Hall mass can be described by a conventional Wannier decomposition (see Table 6),

ΓPSG=Γ2h+Γ3h+Γ4h+Γ1e,\Gamma^{\mathrm{PSG}}=\Gamma^{h}_{2}+\Gamma^{h}_{3}+\Gamma^{h}_{4}+\Gamma_{1}^{e}\,, (181)

which leads to the same Berry phase contributions as the Nf=12N_{f}=12 DSL.

With Nf=4N_{f}=4, there are

(42)=6{{4}\choose{2}}=6 (182)

fundamental monopoles, which are strongly relevant and transform under the global symmetry

SU​(4)f×U​(1)topℤ4.\frac{\mathrm{SU}(4)_{f}\times\mathrm{U}(1)_{\mathrm{top}}}{\mathbb{Z}_{4}}\,. (183)

In particular, the monopoles organize as an SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SO}(6) vector under SU⁡(4)/ℤ2≃SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SU}(4)/\mathbb{Z}_{2}\simeq\mathrm{SO}(6). The monopoles, with SO⁡(6)\mathrm{SO}(6) vector indices, transform as in Table 7.

Thus, two monopoles, Φ1,2\Phi_{1,2}, are symmetry trivial and their real and imaginary parts form a four dimensional allowed subspace of monopole operators. Together with the symmetry-allowed valley Hall mass, namely a Dirac mass with opposite signs in the two valleys that is already present at mean-field level, this shows that the Nf=4N_{f}=4 DSL is not a stable phase. If the monopoles proliferate, the resulting confined phase is expected to spontaneously break the residual (anomalous) SO⁡(4)\mathrm{SO}(4) IR symmetry, as in related examples [74].

Data availability

Machine-readable tables of all C6C_{6}, momentum-star, and time-reversal coefficient multiplicities reported in this work are openly available in the Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22067874.

Code availability

The Mathematica notebook used for the 924924-dimensional monopole classification, together with two mutually independent Python verification programs that reconstruct the exterior-power representation and perform automated dimension and group-algebra checks, is openly available in the Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22067874.
